contentHtml:
Dr Gowri Kulkarni, Chief Medical Officer, MediBuddy, explains how seemingly minor increases in blood pressure, blood sugar and cholesterol can build into serious stroke risks over time and why routine consultations are critical to catching them early

A blood pressure reading that is slightly high or a borderline blood sugar report rarely changes someone’s day. As long as there is no discomfort, work, family responsibilities and daily routines take priority. Without pain or visible symptoms, these findings are easy to put aside. But feeling healthy does not necessarily mean being free of risk, particularly when several health indicators are gradually moving in the wrong direction.

Stroke is closer to everyday life than many people realise. The World Health Organization (WHO) estimates that 11.9 million people experienced a new stroke worldwide in 2021, while 93.8 million were living with its effects. Over the past two decades, the lifetime risk of stroke has increased by 50 per cent. Today, one in four adults is expected to experience a stroke during their lifetime. What makes this particularly concerning is that many of the factors behind these events, including high blood pressure, smoking, high cholesterol, raised blood sugar and physical inactivity, can be identified and addressed well before an emergency occurs.

When a stroke occurs, every minute matters. Sudden facial drooping, weakness in an arm or leg, difficulty speaking, loss of vision or trouble with balance requires immediate medical attention. For eligible patients whose stroke is caused by a blood clot, doctors can administer clot-dissolving medication within 4.5 hours of symptoms beginning. This critical period is often referred to as the “golden window” for stroke treatment. Some carefully selected patients may also benefit from clot-removal treatment within 24 hours, depending on clinical assessment and brain imaging. These treatment windows make reaching a hospital quickly critical, but prevention must begin much earlier.

India’s hospital-based National Stroke Registry Programme, which analysed 34,792 cases across 30 centres, found that 13.8 per cent of patients were below 45 years of age. Nearly one in seven patients in the study was a young adult. The finding challenges the idea that stroke is something to worry about only in old age and reinforces why risk factors need attention much earlier in life.

The risks are often hiding in everyday health records

According to the WHO, ten major modifiable risk factors contribute to stroke. These range from medical conditions such as high blood pressure, high LDL cholesterol, raised blood glucose and kidney dysfunction to lifestyle and environmental factors such as smoking, excess salt consumption, physical inactivity, harmful alcohol use and air pollution. This is important because stroke prevention cannot be reduced to monitoring one health indicator. It requires looking at the wider picture of a person’s health and daily habits.

The CII–MediBuddy report, Workplace Health Reimagined, highlights a gap in preventive care: 52 per cent of employees who receive a health check-up do not act on its findings. While not stroke-specific, this shows why identifying a risk is only the first step. A raised blood pressure reading or abnormal blood sugar result matters only when it leads to follow-up.

These risks rarely appear alone. High blood pressure may coexist with rising blood sugar, abnormal cholesterol or limited physical activity. Managed separately, these concerns may seem less significant. Together, however, they can point to a wider cardiovascular risk. Healthcare providers need to connect the findings rather than view each reading in isolation.

Make every OPD consultation count

A patient may visit a doctor for something as routine as a headache, a digestive problem or recurring fatigue. While addressing the immediate complaint, the doctor may also notice a blood pressure reading that is consistently high or a previous blood sugar report that needs follow-up. These details may seem unrelated to the reason for the visit, but they could offer an opportunity to identify risks much earlier.

Stroke prevention should not begin only when a patient develops neurological symptoms or is identified as high-risk. It needs to become part of routine outpatient consultations and chronic disease reviews. This calls for a more consistent approach to screening. Depending on a patient’s age and medical history, routine assessments can include blood pressure, BMI and waist circumference, tobacco and alcohol use, and personal or family history of cardiovascular disease or stroke. Diabetes and lipid screening can be recommended based on clinical risk. Questions about physical activity, diet and sleep can help doctors understand habits that may be contributing to the patient’s overall risk.

Turn findings into follow-through

Even after a risk is identified, patients may miss medication doses, postpone follow-up visits or continue with prescriptions that are no longer adequately controlling their condition. Medication reconciliation, adherence counselling, prescription reviews and refill reminders can help address these gaps. When treatment targets are not achieved, the care plan needs to be reassessed rather than allowing uncontrolled conditions to persist. Patients must also understand why continuing treatment matters, even when they feel perfectly well.

Lifestyle changes need to be part of this plan, too. Advice on nutrition, physical activity, tobacco cessation, sleep and alcohol consumption should be practical enough to fit into everyday life, with attention to mental health and stress.

Ultimately, stroke prevention cannot be left to neurologists or specialist hospitals alone. Primary care doctors, OPD services, chronic care teams, specialists and patients all have a role. A stroke may occur suddenly, but the risks that contribute to it often develop over years. Every routine consultation is an opportunity to recognise those risks, connect the dots and act before they lead to an emergency.
